title: Delivering Silicon Systems Through AI Disruption, Part 2: The Conductor
gist: Joel Jorgensen argues that AI speeding up one layer of a chip development flow (technical work, tools, social circuitry) breaks the overall flow unless an operating model, the 'conductor', sets tempo, cues handoffs, balances resources and listens via inline monitors. He prescribes fab-style workflow owners, nested ownership up to portfolio level, and measuring dates and cycle time rather than tokens or lines of code.

insights.claim: When AI speeds up only one layer of a semiconductor development flow while other layers cannot keep up, the overall flow does not get faster but falls apart.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Local AI productivity gains in chip design may not translate into faster tape-outs; bottlenecks shift elsewhere.
insights.quote: That’s what happens when AI speeds up one layer of a development flow and the other layers can’t keep up.

insights.claim: Chip companies rigorously margin, simulate and verify every signal path on silicon but never designed the path work takes from architecture to design to test, which is why AI feels so disruptive.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Firms that engineer their workflows may capture AI gains that peers lose to process friction.
insights.quote: I think part of the reason AI feels so disruptive is that we never designed our development flows the way we design our circuits.

insights.claim: Harvard Business School's Karim Lakhani, in the foreword to Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index, warns that agents can accelerate work but also expose brittle processes, unclear decision rights and weak governance.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Governance and process maturity become a differentiator in enterprise agent adoption.
insights.quote: “Agents can accelerate work, but they can also expose brittle processes, unclear decision rights, and weak governance.”

insights.claim: Everyone is getting the same AI tools, so competitive advantage in delivering silicon will come from the operating model (a designed workflow plus a conductor), not tool access.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: AI tooling is commoditizing; execution discipline, not tool choice, separates winners.
insights.quote: Everyone is getting the same AI tools.

insights.claim: The author's 'conductor' operating model for development flows has four jobs: set program tempo and committed dates, cue each section with clear readiness signals (e.g., RTL ready for verification), balance AI, people, compute and licenses across teams, and listen for drift.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: A checklist for evaluating whether a chip team can absorb AI tooling without missing schedules.

insights.claim: Leaders must experience the work live, in labs and regular team meetings, to hear drift, yet this is the first thing squeezed out of a leader's calendar.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Management bandwidth is a hidden constraint on AI-driven process change.

insights.claim: Milestone reviews months apart look at task completion, leaving leaders blind to idle work between milestones, while status updates get sanitized as issues travel up the organization.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Program-level schedule risk in chip development is systematically under-reported.
insights.quote: By the time an issue works its way up the org to the program meeting, it’s been sanitized.

insights.claim: Inline monitors, signals built into the work like control charts on a fab line, show where work is waiting and whether the date is moving weeks before a milestone review would.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Opportunity for EDA/flow-analytics tools that instrument development workflows.
insights.quote: Inline monitors report what’s actually happening, not what somebody decided to say about it.

insights.claim: Example inline monitors by layer: bug count and late spec changes for technical work; test time and license/compute wait time for tools; bug open-to-close time and milestone checklist status for social circuitry.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: License and compute wait time are flagged as measurable bottlenecks, relevant to EDA licensing and compute providers.

insights.claim: Teams should run redesigned AI workflows against a baseline and measure schedule date and cycle time, not tokens or lines of code.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Token and LOC metrics overstate AI value; investors should look for cycle-time evidence.
insights.quote: Measure the date and the cycle time, not tokens or lines of code.

insights.claim: Like fab modules where an etch owner designs, monitors and improves the etch process, every development workflow needs an owner who reviews its monitors on a regular cadence and acts on them.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Importing fab-style process ownership into design organizations is a concrete management lever.

insights.claim: Cross-functional flows such as firmware-versus-hardware disputes need an owner with tie-breaking authority, otherwise issues are decided by seniority, the loudest voice or whoever is least behind schedule.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Unresolved hardware/firmware handoffs remain a major source of program slips.

insights.claim: Microsoft's report raises three AI governance questions: who reviews agent performance, who can update the workflows agents run, and how a local win gets captured and scaled across the organization.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Agent governance is an emerging enterprise need and possible product category.
insights.quote: “Who reviews agent performance? Who has the authority to update the workflows that agents run?

insights.claim: VerifAIX's Madhulima Tewari argued at SEMICON West that the system generating an artifact cannot be the only one certifying it: the LLM proposes and deterministic engines decide.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Supports durable demand for deterministic EDA verification engines alongside generative AI.
insights.quote: The LLM proposes, and deterministic engines decide.

themes.theme: Nested hierarchy and scaling local wins

insights.claim: Development flows should be nested like SoC hierarchies: workflows owned at block and team level roll up to the program (conducted by a Director) and programs to the portfolio (conducted by a VP), so a local win becomes how every team works.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Explains how AI process gains scale (or fail to) across large semiconductor organizations.

insights.claim: Because tools, teams and AI are changing the work weekly, a flow without someone listening at each level can run away in ways no single person can see.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Rapid AI change raises execution-risk variance across chip programs.

insights.claim: In a fab anecdote, a lead lot whose prior best was 35 days, with a 25-day goal, came out in 22 days under a shepherding principal engineer, and a year later 25 days was the average with no shepherding needed.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Shows that orchestrated process improvement can cut cycle time roughly a third and become self-sustaining.
